claims.text: Conventional homogeneous alloy microstructures exhibit an inverse relationship between strength and ductility.
Machine-learning models can correlate processing conditions with gradient grain size, phase distributions, and interface coherency.
Machine-learning-guided thermo-mechanical processing can produce heterogeneous or gradient microstructures.
Heterogeneous microstructures with engineered phase distributions can support concurrent high strength and high ductility.
Gradient grain-size variations contribute to concurrent strength and ductility improvement.
A machine-learning-guided processing strategy that creates heterogeneous or gradient microstructures will overcome the conventional strength-ductility trade-off in structural alloys.
The proposed strategy can be implemented through standard casting or rolling with machine-learning-optimized processing parameters.
The targeted strength-ductility improvement applies at room temperature.
Engineered gradient microstructures promote strain partitioning.
Engineered gradient microstructures activate additional deformation mechanisms.
Strain partitioning and additional deformation mechanisms delay necking.
The engineered microstructure preserves barriers to dislocation motion and therefore maintains strength.
Coherent engineered interfaces can facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations that otherwise cause premature cracking.
Machine-learning-optimized gradient structures will increase tensile strength without reducing ductility relative to conventionally processed homogeneous counterparts.
High-strength alloys typically have low ductility, and high-ductility alloys typically have low strength.
Homogeneous microstructural characteristics cause the conventional strength-ductility trade-off.
The magnitude of strength and ductility improvement depends on the accuracy of the machine-learning predictions.
The magnitude of improvement depends on achievable control over processing parameters.
Processing heterogeneities not captured by the model may limit performance gains.
